questions.scenario: Consider a simple algorithm that sorts an array of integers using the bubble sort method.
questions.question: Explain why bubble sort is not the most efficient sorting algorithm for large arrays.
marking_criteria: Explanation of the time complexity of bubble sort.
Comparison with other sorting algorithms.
Reasoning about efficiency for large arrays.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why bubble sort is not the most efficient sorting algorithm for large arrays — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Comparison with other sorting.
questions.model_answer: Bubble sort has a time complexity of O(n^2) in both the worst and average cases, where n is the number of items being sorted. This means that the number of comparisons and swaps grows quadratically with the size of the array. For large arrays, this makes bubble sort inefficient compared to algorithms like quicksort or mergesort, which have better average-case time complexities of O(n log n).

questions.scenario: Consider a simple algorithm that sorts an array of integers using the selection sort method.
questions.question: Describe the selection sort algorithm.
marking_criteria: Identify the basic concept of selection sort.
Explain the process of finding the minimum element.
Describe the swapping of elements.
hints: Start by explaining the overall approach of selection sort.
questions.model_answer: The selection sort algorithm works by repeatedly finding the minimum element from the unsorted part of the array and putting it at the beginning. The array is divided into two parts: the sorted part at the left end and the unsorted part at the right end. Initially, the sorted part is empty and the unsorted part is the entire array. The algorithm finds the minimum element in the unsorted part and swaps it with the leftmost element of the unsorted part. This process is repeated until the entire array is sorted.
questions.explanation: Describe the step-by-step process of how the selection sort algorithm works to sort an array of integers.

questions.question: Explain why the binary search algorithm is efficient for large sorted arrays.

Discuss the logarithmic time complexity.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the binary search algorithm is efficient for large sorted arrays — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Discuss the time complexity.
questions.model_answer: The binary search algorithm is efficient for large sorted arrays because it reduces the search space by half with each iteration. Total count of comparisons made during the entire process.

questions.model_answer:
To sort the array [7, 3, 5, 8, 2] using insertion sort, we start with the sorted section [7] and the unsorted section [3, 5, 8, 2].

1. Insert 3 into the sorted section: 1 comparison (3 < 7).
2. Insert 5 into the sorted section [3, 7]: 1 comparison (5 < 7), 1 comparison (5 < 3).
3. Insert 8 into the sorted section [3, 5, 7]: 1 comparison (8 > 7), no shift.
4. Insert 2 into the sorted section [3, 5, 7, 8]: 1 comparison (2 < 8), 1 comparison (2 < 7), 1 comparison (2 < 5), 1 comparison (2 < 3).

Total comparisons: 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 8.

questions.model_answer: Insertion sort has a time complexity of O(n^2) in both the worst and average cases, where n is the number of elements in the array. This makes it inefficient for large arrays because the number of comparisons and shifts grows quadratically with the size of the array. Other sorting algorithms like merge sort and quicksort have better average-case time complexities of O(n log n), making them more efficient for large datasets. Insertion sort performs poorly on nearly sorted or reverse-sorted arrays, as it still requires a significant number of comparisons and shifts.
questions.explanation: Explain the time complexity of insertion sort and compare it with other sorting algorithms to highlight its inefficiencies for large arrays.
